The verb must match the real who. One thing gets is, has, or a verb ending in s. Many things get are, have, and no s.
The trick is to X ray the sentence. See through the extra words in the middle to find the real who.
Here's the method. If the choices are forms of the same verb, cross out the middle words, find the who, and count it: one or many.
The collection of rare letters blank kept in a vault. Cross out of rare letters. The who is the collection. One thing, so the verb is is.
Trap alert. The plural verb, are, matches letters, the word right before the blank. But letters is inside the of phrase. Don't match the nearest noun.
Two subjects joined by and make many. The botanist and the chemist are on the panel. A plus B equals two.
But along with and as well as are just extra. The director, along with her assistants, is arriving. The who is one director.
Each means one. Each of the samples has a label. And with there is or there are, the who comes after the verb. There are three reasons.
Let's try an SAT style question. Throat singing, a tradition with two performers, blank, an advocate. Has found, or find?
X ray it. Cross out the part between the dashes. Throat singing has found an advocate. Throat singing is one thing.
Trap alert. Two performers is plural, but it's inside the dashes. It's extra. The who is still throat singing.
Your turn. Pause the video. The list of ingredients, blank, on the back of the box. Is, or are?
Is. Cross out of ingredients. The who is the list, and it's one list.
Remember three things. Cross out the middle. Find the real who, then count it. And never match the noun right before the verb. Great work.
